Note that the Cambridge Indicator variable was not statistically significant in both nighttime models for the before and after LED periods at the 0.05 level of significance. This indicates that with and without the LED system, both cities did not have significantly different crash frequencies during nighttime. Both of the daytime models, however, showed that the Cambridge Indicator variable was significant with a positive parameter, indicating Cambridge had higher daytime crashes compared to Somerville. When comparing the parameters for the Cambridge Indicator variable in the two daytime models, the parameter for the after LED conversion model (0.47) was noticeably larger than that for the before-LED conversion model (0.22). The larger parameter for the after LED conversion model suggests that, during the after-LED conversion period, Cambridge had more daytime crashes when statistically controlling by changes in the Somerville crashes. The fact that the city indicator variable was not significant in the nighttime models potentially indicates that the LED system at Cambridge functioned well in reducing the higher nighttime crash frequencies in the city when using Somerville as the basis. 55 Table 13. This analysis included the following models: • Local streets after 8:00 p.m. for after LED conversion. These are two models analyzing ND crash ratios for nighttime crashes occurring after 8:00 p.m. on local roadways in Somerville and C3 roadways in Cambridge. One model was developed for the period after the LED conversion (5a) and another for the before period (5b). Both models were developed using linear regression with mixed effects. The purpose of these two models was to compare the city parameter to identify potential differences in ND crash ratios between the two cities that could indicate effects due to dimmed lighting levels. • C2 roadways for nighttime crashes after 10:00 p.m.
